concept.name: Autocorrelation
concept.definition: The correlation of a time series with itself at different time lags: a measure of how strongly an observation is linearly related to observations h periods earlier or later. Significant nonzero autocorrelation means the series is not random white noise.
concept.intuition: Autocorrelation asks: does a high value today tend to be followed by high values tomorrow (positive) or by low values (negative), or is there no relationship at all?
concept.mechanics: The sample autocorrelation at lag h is R_h = C_h / C_0, where C_h = (1/N)*sum_{t=1}^{N-h}(Y_t - mean)(Y_{t+h} - mean) is the sample autocovariance and C_0 the sample variance. Under randomness, autocorrelations should lie within bands of about +/-z_{1-alpha/2}/sqrt(N); systematic patterns signal structure and are used to identify AR/MA model orders.
concept.formula: R_h = C_h / C_0, with C_h = (1/N) * sum_{t=1}^{N-h} (Y_t - Ybar)(Y_{t+h} - Ybar); R_h lies in [-1, 1].
concept.failure_modes: Absence of autocorrelation does not imply randomness: nonlinear dependence (e.g., volatility clustering in squared returns) survives zero linear autocorrelation. In non-stationary series, sample autocorrelations are spuriously large and slow-decaying.
concept.misconceptions: That zero autocorrelation proves independence (uncorrelated is not independent), and that significant daily-return autocorrelation in stock indexes is directly exploitable profit after transaction costs (usually it is not).
concept.example: The autocorrelation plot of a strongly autoregressive series shows large positive R_1 decaying gradually; the same plot for white noise shows all R_h near zero within the 95% bands.

citations.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, Section 1.3.3.1 Autocorrelation Plot
